write.desc: This topic carries the epsilon-style limit from sequences over to functions, uses it to define continuity, and proves the big theorems about continuous functions (extreme value, intermediate value, uniform continuity) together with the results on monotone functions and their inverses; the points belong together because each rests on the same definition of a functional limit and its sequential form.

points.name: The epsilon-delta limit of a function
points.what: The learner can state the definition of lim_{x->c} f(x) = L for a function on a set A and a limit point c of A, explain why c must be a limit point, and explain why the value f(c), or whether it exists, plays no part.
outside: limit (accumulation) point of a set of reals
absolute value and the triangle inequality
nested quantifiers and their order

points.name: Proving functional limits from the definition
points.what: The learner can do scratch work to find a delta that depends on epsilon and on the point c (for example for x^2, 1/x and sqrt x), use the delta = min(1, ...) trick to bound a factor first, and write the final proof cleanly.
outside: bounding techniques for inequalities ('it suffices to show')
separating scratch work from the final proof write-up

points.name: The sequential criterion for functional limits
points.what: The learner can prove that f(x) -> L as x -> c exactly when f(x_n) -> L for every sequence x_n in the domain with x_n != c and x_n -> c, including the converse by contradiction with delta = 1/n.
outside: epsilon-N definition of the limit of a sequence
negating nested quantified statements
proof by contradiction

points.name: Showing that a functional limit does not exist
points.what: The learner can write the negation of the limit definition and prove non-existence by finding two sequences tending to c whose images have different limits, as for sin(1/x) at 0 or the sign function at 0.
outside: negating nested quantified statements

points.name: Limit laws and the squeeze theorem for functions
points.what: The learner can prove the sum, product and quotient laws and the order and squeeze theorems for functional limits by transferring the sequence results through the sequential criterion, and use them to evaluate limits rigorously.
outside: algebraic limit theorem for sequences (sum, product, quotient)
order and squeeze theorems for sequences

points.name: One-sided limits
points.what: The learner can define left and right limits by restricting the domain, and prove that the two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

points.name: Limits at infinity and infinite limits
points.what: The learner can define and prove statements such as lim_{x->infinity} f(x) = L and lim_{x->c} f(x) = infinity with the right quantifiers (M or N in place of epsilon or delta), and recognise the matching sequential versions.
outside: extended reals notation (plus and minus infinity)
divergence of a sequence to infinity

points.name: Continuity at a point
points.what: The learner can state the epsilon-delta and sequential definitions of continuity at a point of the domain, prove they are equivalent, see that a function is automatically continuous at isolated points, and relate continuity at a limit point to lim_{x->c} f(x) = f(c).
outside: isolated point of a set

points.name: Algebra and composition of continuous functions
points.what: The learner can prove that sums, products, quotients (where the denominator is nonzero) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and conclude that polynomials and rational functions are continuous on their domains.

points.name: Types of discontinuity and standard examples
points.what: The learner can classify a discontinuity as removable, jump or essential, and prove the behaviour of the standard examples: the Dirichlet function (discontinuous everywhere), x times the Dirichlet function (continuous only at 0), sin(1/x) (essential at 0) and x sin(1/x) (removable at 0).
outside: density of the rationals and irrationals in the reals

points.name: Thomae's function
points.what: The learner can prove that Thomae's function (1/q at p/q in lowest terms, 0 at irrationals) is continuous at every irrational and discontinuous at every rational, using that only finitely many fractions with small denominators lie near a point.
outside: density of the rationals and irrationals in the reals
Archimedean property

points.name: Continuous images of compact sets
points.what: The learner can prove that a continuous function maps compact sets to compact sets, using sequential compactness, and give examples showing the image of a non-compact set need not be compact.
outside: sequential compactness of a set of reals
subsequences and the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem

points.name: The extreme value theorem
points.what: The learner can prove that a continuous function on a nonempty compact set (in particular on [a,b]) attains a maximum and a minimum, and give counterexamples when the set is open, unbounded or the function is discontinuous.
outside: supremum and infimum
Heine-Borel theorem (compact means closed and bounded)

points.name: The intermediate value theorem
points.what: The learner can prove that a continuous function on an interval takes every value between any two of its values, both via connectedness (continuous images of connected sets are connected) and via the supremum of the set where f < y, and show the theorem fails without continuity or on a non-interval.
outside: connected sets and that the connected subsets of the reals are the intervals
completeness axiom and the epsilon characterisation of the supremum

points.name: Applications of the intermediate value theorem
points.what: The learner can use the intermediate value theorem to prove existence results: every odd-degree polynomial has a real root, a continuous map of [a,b] into itself has a fixed point, and every positive number has an n-th root.

points.name: Uniform continuity
points.what: The learner can state uniform continuity and explain, by comparing the order of the quantifiers, how it differs from continuity at every point (delta may depend on epsilon only, not on the point); they can prove functions are or are not uniformly continuous, for example x^2 on R and 1/x on (0,1), using the sequential criterion for failure.
outside: nested quantifiers and why their order matters
negating nested quantified statements

points.name: Lipschitz functions
points.what: The learner can define Lipschitz functions, prove that Lipschitz functions are uniformly continuous, and show the converse fails with sqrt x on [0, infinity).

points.name: The Heine-Cantor theorem
points.what: The learner can prove that a continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous (by contradiction with Bolzano-Weierstrass), and explain why compactness is the hypothesis that turns pointwise deltas into one delta.
outside: sequential compactness of a set of reals
subsequences and the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem

points.name: One-sided limits of monotone functions
points.what: The learner can prove that a monotone function has one-sided limits at every point, equal to a supremum or infimum of its values on one side, so that its only possible discontinuities are jumps.
outside: supremum and infimum and their epsilon characterisation

points.name: Discontinuities of a monotone function are countable
points.what: The learner can prove that a monotone function has at most countably many discontinuities by choosing a distinct rational inside each jump.
outside: countable and uncountable sets
density of the rationals in the reals

points.name: Continuity of inverse functions
points.what: The learner can prove that a continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone, and that the inverse of a continuous strictly monotone function on an interval is continuous, with n-th roots as the main example.
outside: inverse of a bijective function

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed., Springer)
where.detail: Chapter 4, Functional Limits and Continuity (4.2 functional limits, 4.3 continuous functions, 4.4 continuous functions on compact sets, 4.5 intermediate value theorem, 4.6 sets of discontinuity)

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Chapter 4, Limits, and Chapter 5, Continuous Functions (5.3 continuous functions on intervals, 5.4 uniform continuity, 5.6 monotone and inverse functions)

where.title: Michael Spivak, Calculus
where.detail: Chapters 5 to 8: Limits, Continuous Functions, Three Hard Theorems, Least Upper Bounds (uniform continuity in Chapter 8)

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 4, Continuity (limits of functions, continuity and compactness, connectedness, discontinuities, monotonic functions)
